How coarse must coordinates be to protect a site? The grain table answers in metres, not vibes.
“Supplied at 6 decimal places” in a contract means 0.11 m grain — this page is the translation the lawyers needed.
Latitude grain by places: 3 → ~111 m, 4 → ~11 m, 5 → ~1.1 m, 6 → ~0.11 m, 7 → ~0.011 m. Each place divides the claim by ten — the most ruthless exchange rate in mapping.
At 60° latitude the longitude grain halves (a degree is 55.8 km there). The calculator's latitude input exists because 'a decimal place' is not one size on a round planet.

faq: What does this tool calculate?
The ground size of one unit in the last decimal place — for latitude and longitude at a stated latitude — from WGS84 degree lengths.
Do I need an account?
No — places and latitude in, grain out.
Can I rely on this for professional work?
The grain arithmetic is exact geometry — rely on it. Professional judgment is matching the places to the instrument, which the table guides.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84 degree lengths throughout.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
No — this calculator is the standing refutation, with numbers: places measure resolution, instruments measure accuracy, and the two meet only when chosen honestly.
Why does latitude matter?
Longitude degrees shrink toward the poles, so a decimal place of longitude is worth fewer metres at 60° than at the equator. Latitude's grain is nearly constant.
Cell versus error?
Grain is the grid's mesh, not the fix's error. A 5-place coordinate from a 10-metre fix claims a 1.1 m mesh while sitting up to 10 m off — both numbers can be true.
What about DMS seconds?
Same logic in sexagesimal: 0.1″ ≈ 3 m, 0.01″ ≈ 0.3 m — the Arcseconds to Ground Distance Calculator prices those.
Fuzzing for privacy?
2–3 places (1.1 km–111 m) is the customary publication fuzz. Size the choice here, apply it in the precision tool.
Trailing zeros meaningful?
They declare the grain: 40.7580 claims 11 m dress; 40.758 claims 111 m. Honest dressers keep the zero.
Mars coordinates?
Different planet, different degree lengths — a charming question this Earth-bound calculator declines.
